newsitem.title: UK: Billiton issue looks pricey, analysts say.
newsitem.headline: Billiton issue looks pricey, analysts say.

text.p: Mining group Billiton is aiming to come to the London Stock Exchange at a price many analysts here consider too high to warrant a "buy" recommendation.
While they generally believe Billiton's share issue will hit within the target range, they don't see much upside potential after the placing next week.
Base metals group Billiton will be demerged from South Africa's Gencor Ltd, while it also plans to issue about 375 million new shares between 210 to 240 pence a share.
The price, which will be announced early on Tuesday, will likely be at the bottom of the range, said Roger Chaplin at T. Hoare & Co.
This would mean Billiton shares will trade sideways at best over the next couple of months, he said.
"On our valuation and the outlook for growth in Billiton's businesses, we see little upside potential for the shares," Chaplin and other Hoare analysts wrote in a recent report.

With a market capitalisation between 4.4 billion and 5.1 billion pounds ($8.5 billion), Billiton will become a London blue chip, making it an attractive investment alternative to mining giant Rio Tinto.
But Rio Tinto has already secured strong growth with many projects set to come to fruition soon, analysts said.

In contrast, Billiton has to buy in its growth prospects, which always carries the risk that the company - though widely considered to be very well managed - is too eager to buy and therefore overpays.
Analysts also point to the risks stemming from the fact 70 percent of Billiton's assets are in South Africa.
By comparison, 80 percent of Rio Tinto's assets are based in more stable, first world countries, such as the United States and Australia.
"There is a higher currency risk as well as political uncertainty with Billiton," said one analyst, who declined to be named.
Others add Rio Tinto also has better quality assets with Chaplin saying Billiton has some rather poor aluminium operations.
For these reasons, industry watchers believe Billiton should be trading at price-to-earnings ratio which should be 10 to 15 percent lower than Rio Tinto's.
But even at the lowest suggested price, Billiton would be trading at 18.3 times, based on estimated 1997 earnings of 11.5 pence per share, the Hoare report said.
This would be well above the P/E ratio for Rio Tinto of 17.7 times 1997 consensus earnings.
"People are paying for Billiton for more than just the existing assets," said Emile Morfett at Paribas Capital markets.
"They are paying a premium for the management and a premium for future acquisitions and I think that the pricing is too rich," he added.
Morfett will only be interested in buying Billiton below 200 pence a share.
At higher levels he recommends switching into either Rio Tinto or Minorco SA, the South African group listed in Luxembourg.
Morfett nevertheless predicts a smooth share placement at levels near 210 pence. He sees keen interest particularly from investment funds who are obliged to invest in FTSE 100 stocks.
But with the FTSE trading near all-time highs, he also sees selling pressure coming from South African investors, who will make up about 80 percent of shareholders.
"The South African institutes who have been nursing the stock for many years, may be selling into strength," Morfett said. ($ = 0.598 British Pounds)
